source.title: The emergence of sparse attention: impact of data distribution and benefits of repetition
source.authors: Nicolas Zucchet; Francesco D'Angelo; Andrew Kyle Lampinen; S. C. Chan

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports training dynamics on synthetic attention and associative recall tasks, but does not test training classification error on CIFAR, spurious minima, shortcuts, initialization schemes, learning-rate stability, or batch normalization as described in the versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own training and evaluation outcomes on toy linear-regression and associative-recall tasks. These concern emergence timing and repetition, not the training-error outcomes named by the claim versions. The paper's discussion of prior work is not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study measures sparse-attention emergence and how repetition, task difficulty, architecture and optimizer affect its timing. It does not test any of V1–V6. Its Hessian analysis concerns gradient flow without a finite learning-rate stability threshold; its architecture sweep does not compare plain and residual convolutional networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute abrupt learning transitions to interactions between feedforward learning and sparse attention, find emergence timing sensitive to data, architecture and optimizer, and show that repetition accelerates learning while sometimes impairing generalization. Extension to large models and realistic distributions remains unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates emergence timing in synthetic regression and associative-recall tasks, rather than benchmark classification error or the interventions in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Emergence timing changes with sequence length, dimension or vocabulary size, repetition, optimizer, number of heads, task position information, and architecture. In associative recall, high repetition can impair generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse-attention regression exhibits an initial loss plateau whose duration increases with sequence length and dimension. Repetition accelerates escape; cross-sample repetition can slow later convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data structure and repetition control sparse-attention emergence timing in synthetic regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformer emergence timing depends on optimizer and architecture; Adam substantially outpaces SGD, and additional heads lengthen plateaus more than additional layers in the tested sweep.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer and architecture affect the timing and scaling of sparse-attention learning on synthetic tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Associative-recall emergence slows with sequence length and vocabulary size. Repetition accelerates emergence, with reported factors of four and two, but stronger repetition can impair generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repetition can accelerate associative-recall learning while introducing a trade-off with generalization.

record.problems: The empirical tasks are synthetic and small scale. Results chiefly concern emergence timing rather than final training error. Some difficult settings did not reach the transition within the allotted 50k steps. The authors note that cross-sample repetition makes plateau measurement harder, and that it did not admit an accurate power-law fit in one reported experiment.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct reported conditions were extracted beyond the selected task and repetition comparisons, architecture sweep, and optimizer comparison.

untested.parts: All parts: convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/100, including random labels and recipe or capacity effects.
All parts: two-layer ReLU teacher-student spurious minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
All parts: depth degradation in plain convolutional networks, identity-shortcut comparisons, and the stated initialization exceptions.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and trainable depth.
All parts: recovery above initial stability thresholds, finite-step edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to those thresholds.
All parts: batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix A.1 explicitly excludes edge-of-stability phenomena through its gradient-flow assumption. Figure 8's Hessian dynamics and discussion of possible discrete-time learning-rate constraints do not establish V5. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6; this does not dispute the reported emergence effects.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 classification error; random or corrupted labels; model size, optimizer, training duration, and regularization effects on training error.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual networks' training error across depth; shortcut effects; deep tanh and normalization-free residual training.
Activation-matched or orthogonal initialization effects on learning speed and trainable depth.
Training above stability thresholds, sharpness dynamics, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons for training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: simplified attention-based model
rows.operation_detail: Gradient-flow training on single-location linear regression without repetition; measured time to leave initial loss plateau.
rows.measure: Training-loss phase transition and plateau duration.
rows.value: Initial loss plateau followed by a sharp decrease; plateau duration increases with sequence length T and dimension d.
rows.note: The reported outcome is emergence timing on a synthetic regression task, not classification error.
rows.check: The plateau is observed, but its duration on synthetic attention regression does not measure any claim version.

rows.subject: simplified attention-based model
rows.operation_detail: Gradient-flow training with in-context repetition of the relevant token.
rows.baseline: No repetition condition is the reference.
rows.value: Plateau length fit: Tplateau = 1.51 T^0.99 B^-0.99 (R2 = 0.999).
rows.note: The authors report that increasing B reduces the initial plateau.
rows.check: No version applies. The extracted scaling law omits d^0.49: Figure 2 gives Tplateau = 1.51 T^0.99 B^-0.99 d^0.49.

source_check.problem: The extracted scaling law omits the factor d^0.49.

rows.subject: simplified attention-based model
rows.operation_detail: Gradient-flow training with cross-sample repetition of the relevant token.
rows.measure: Plateau duration and test loss dynamics.
rows.value: Plateau-length fit: Tplateau = 2.15(√(dT) / √(p²d + (1 − p)²))^1.02 (R2 = 0.992); repetition accelerates emergence, including on test data without repetition.
rows.note: The paper also says cross-sample repetition gives only a temporary advantage and can slow long-run learning.
rows.check: No version applies. Correct the numerator inside the fitted expression from sqrt(dT) to T sqrt(d), as established by Appendix A.4.2: Tplateau = 2.15[T sqrt(d)/sqrt(p²d + (1−p)²)]^1.02.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 2 caption; Section 2.3; Appendix A.4.2, eigenvalues and exit-time scaling.
source_check.problem: The numerator is T sqrt(d), rather than sqrt(dT).

rows.subject: 2-layer 4-head Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Adam training on the single-location linear-regression variant; layer normalization removed.
rows.value: Loss shows a sharp phase transition; repetition accelerates emergence. Replacing Adam with SGD substantially slows emergence and increases dependence on task difficulty.
rows.note: The results concern synthetic-task plateau timing. Figure 15 reports separate fitted scaling laws for SGD and Adam.
rows.check: No version applies. Split the default two-layer, four-head results from the optimizer comparison: Figure 15 uses a single-layer, single-head Transformer, SGD at 5×10^-3 versus Adam at 10^-4.

source_check.correct: Sections 2.4 and Figure 3 use a two-layer, four-head Transformer trained with Adam at 10^-4, without layer normalization. Figure 15 compares a single-layer, single-head Transformer trained with SGD at 5×10^-3 versus Adam at 10^-4; Adam substantially accelerates emergence.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.4; Appendix B.3; Figure 15 caption; Appendix D.3.
source_check.problem: The row combines default two-layer, four-head results with an optimizer comparison conducted on a single-layer, single-head model.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Training on the in-context associative-recall task and evaluating on data without repetition.
rows.measure: Test accuracy emergence and plateau duration.
rows.value: In-context repetition speeds emergence by a factor of 4; larger repetition can overfit, with test accuracy eventually increasing late in training for large repetition amounts.
rows.note: The authors describe overfitting risk at larger repetition levels and late grokking-like increases.
rows.check: Faster emergence and impaired generalization under repetition do not measure any version; partial is not a claim-relative state here.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Transformer training with varying layer and head counts on the single-location linear-regression task.

conditions.value: number of layers and heads varied

rows.value: Increasing the number of heads increased plateau length more significantly than increasing depth; fit: Tplateau = 1.03 d^1.27 T^0.70 Nlayers^0.06 Nheads^0.16 (R2 = 0.995).
rows.note: This is a task-specific learning-time result, not a comparison of training classification error.
rows.check: The head/depth sweep measures plateau duration in residual Transformers at an untuned learning rate. It does not test V2's spurious minima or V3's plain-versus-residual training-error comparison.
